standard.title: Causes of the Second World War
standard.description: the causes, outbreak and course of the Second World War and the significance of Australian involvement
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have explained the causes of World War One using the MAIN framework (Militarism, Alliance systems, Imperialism, Nationalism) and can distinguish long-term structural causes from short-term triggers (AC9HH9K08). They have examined the effects of WW1 on Australian society including conscription debates and Australia's relationship with Britain (AC9HH9K11), and have encountered the Treaty of Versailles as a post-war settlement — though depth of treatment of its specific terms is variable (AC9HH9K12 elaboration). They have not yet examined the inter-war period (1919–1939) as a causal field, the rise of fascism as a structural phenomenon, the diplomatic sequence leading to WW2, or Australia's political decision-making around entry into WW2.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the causes and outbreak of the Second World War across European and Asia-Pacific contexts, analyse the course of the war, and evaluate the significance of Australian involvement.

nodes.label: Inter-war settlement and its instabilities
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how the post-WW1 settlement — the Treaty of Versailles and the League of Nations — created structural conditions of resentment, economic punishment, and failed collective security that formed the necessary preconditions for WW2.
nodes.minimum_width: Students identify at least two specific terms of the Treaty of Versailles and explain why each created conditions of instability or grievance in Germany; explain one structural weakness of the League of Nations.
nodes.typical_width: Students investigate the Treaty of Versailles across its major provisions (territorial concessions, reparations, war guilt clause, military restrictions); explain how each provision produced specific grievances; explain the structural weaknesses of the League of Nations that prevented collective security from functioning; connect the Great Depression to the deepening of economic grievance; distinguish necessary conditions from sufficient causes — the settlement created the conditions but did not make war inevitable.
wider: Examine how the Treaty's terms affected parties beyond Germany — Austria-Hungary successor states, Ottoman successor states, colonial mandate peoples — showing that the grievances enabling instability were systemic, not uniquely German

Investigate the Russian Revolution as a parallel inter-war destabilising force — examining how the emergence of the Soviet Union reshaped European political alignments and contributed to the conditions in which fascism grew

Compare the Paris Peace settlements (Versailles, St Germain, Trianon, Sèvres) as a system — evaluating whether collective security was structurally possible given the contradictions built into the settlement
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who leave this node treating WW2 as simply caused by WW1 — or by Hitler alone — carry a mono-causal framework into every subsequent causal claim. The multi-causal structural conditions established here underpin Nodes 2 and 3: fascism rises in specific soil (N2), and appeasement responds to specific regime character shaped by that soil (N3). Thin treatment here produces systematically flat causal analysis across the unit.
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The inter-war period offers genuine comparative width — the same structural conditions (Depression, weak collective security, nationalist grievance) produced different political outcomes in different countries. Examining these variations builds historical reasoning about contingency and causation that is transferable across the whole unit and beyond.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly collapse complex causation into single-cause explanations (WW1 → Treaty → Hitler → WW2). Structured cause-mapping — categorising causes as economic, political, ideological, structural — builds the multi-causal framework before students are asked to weigh causes. Explicitly distinguishing necessary conditions from sufficient causes is the key scaffold.

Extending Treaty of Versailles analysis across multiple affected parties — and examining how Depression-era conditions produced different political outcomes in different countries — demonstrates that the preconditions for fascism were systemic rather than uniquely German. This corrects the tendency to treat WW2 causes as a specifically German story.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two specific terms of the Treaty of Versailles and explains the link between each term and conditions of grievance or instability in Germany
Explains one structural weakness of the League of Nations and why it undermined collective security in the 1930s

Distinguishes between the Treaty of Versailles as a necessary condition and the outbreak of WW2 as a later outcome — articulating that the settlement created conditions that were subsequently exploited, not an inevitable trajectory

nodes.label: Rise of fascism and militarism as structural responses
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how specific inter-war conditions — economic collapse, institutional failure, ideological grievance — produced the rise of fascist and militarist regimes, and can identify multiple cases demonstrating that this was a systemic phenomenon, not uniquely German.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain two inter-war conditions that contributed to the rise of the Nazi Party in Germany; identify one other fascist or militarist regime (Italy or Japan) and explain its rise in terms of similar conditions.
nodes.typical_width: Students explain how the Great Depression, the failure of Weimar democracy, national humiliation from Versailles, and the appeal of Nazi ideology combined to produce Hitler's rise from 1933; explain the parallel rise of Mussolini's Italy and Imperial Japan as cases of fascism and militarism filling the collective security vacuum; explain how Nazi ideology exploited existing resentments as a political strategy — not merely describe its content.
wider: Examine the ideological contest of the inter-war period — comparing fascism, communism, and liberal democracy as competing responses to post-WWI instability — and analyse why fascism proved more electorally viable than communism in Germany

Investigate the Spanish Civil War (1936–39) as a rehearsal for WW2 — examining how it demonstrated fascist military capability, tested international responses, and anticipated the ideological fault lines of the coming war

Explore the role of propaganda in the consolidation of fascist regimes — examining how Goebbels' media apparatus and Imperial Japan's nationalist education system manufactured consent for expansionist policies
nodes.hinge_reason: All subsequent nodes require a structural understanding of what fascist and militarist regimes were and wanted. Students who explain fascism only as 'Hitler was bad' or 'people were angry after WW1' cannot explain why appeasement seemed rational (N3), why Australia's entry had the political character it did (N4), or why the war's significance extends beyond its events (N5). The Hitler-as-sole-cause misconception, if unresolved here, produces systematically inadequate causal arguments throughout the unit.

response_modes.reason: Introduce ideology as a historical concept explicitly — students need to move from 'events and individuals' to 'ideas and their political effects.' The key scaffold is explaining how Nazi ideology exploited specific existing conditions (economic fear, national humiliation, anti-Semitism) as a deliberate political strategy, not simply describing its content.

Using Italy and Japan as parallel cases alongside Germany is the concrete corrective to Hitler-as-sole-cause. Students who encounter fascism and militarism as a multi-country phenomenon cannot maintain the 'uniquely German pathology' framing.

success_criteria: Explains at least two inter-war conditions that contributed to the rise of the Nazi Party, connecting each condition to a specific political or social mechanism
Identifies one other fascist or militarist regime and explains its rise in terms of inter-war conditions — demonstrating that this was not uniquely German
Explains how Nazi ideology exploited existing resentments as a political strategy, not merely describes its content

nodes.label: The diplomatic sequence and the failure of appeasement
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse the major pre-war events of 1933–1939 as a causal chain in which each failure to respond to aggression made the next act of aggression more likely, and can explain why appeasement was a rational policy that proved catastrophically wrong.
nodes.minimum_width: Students identify three events in the 1933–1939 sequence and explain how each represented an escalation that earlier non-response enabled; explain the appeasement policy and why it failed, using Munich as evidence.
nodes.typical_width: Students trace the escalating sequence across both theatres: Japanese invasion of Manchuria, Italo-Abyssinian Wars, remilitarisation of the Rhineland, Spanish Civil War, annexation of Austria, Munich Agreement and Sudetenland, invasion of Poland (1939), occupation of China; explain appeasement as a rational policy reflecting genuine strategic calculations — fear of another total war, military unpreparedness, trust in Hitler's stated limited aims — and analyse why those assumptions proved wrong; explain why Poland's invasion was the specific trigger for Britain's declaration of war.
wider: Examine the Munich Agreement in depth as a case study in diplomatic failure — analysing Chamberlain's reasoning, Hitler's response, and the historiographical debate over whether appeasement was inevitable or a strategic miscalculation
Compare the timeline of aggression in the European and Asia-Pacific theatres — examining whether the two paths to war were connected or largely independent until 1941

Investigate the role of domestic public opinion and political constraints in Britain and France in limiting governments' responses to fascist aggression — examining how democratic accountability complicated strategic decision-making
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The appeasement case study offers rich historiographical width — students can engage with genuine historical debate about rationality, hindsight bias, and the ethics of diplomatic compromise. The dual-theatre comparison builds analytical skills applicable across the unit.

response_modes.reason: Students need a working repertoire of key pre-war events across both theatres before causal analysis is meaningful. A chronological mapping task — annotating each event with its theatrical context, the aggressor, and the international response — builds the knowledge base that supports the appeasement analysis.

Appeasement as a rational policy that failed requires explicit scaffolding — students default to condemning it as cowardice or weakness. The reasoning scaffold is: what did Chamberlain know? what did he assume? where did his assumptions break down? This is the entry point to genuine historical judgement rather than hindsight condemnation.

success_criteria: Sequences at least three major pre-war events and explains how each contributed to the outbreak of war — not merely lists them
Explains the appeasement policy: what it was, why Western powers adopted it, and what assumptions it made about Hitler's intentions
Explains why the invasion of Poland in 1939 was the specific trigger for Britain's — and therefore Australia's — declaration of war

nodes.label: Australia's entry — political decision, not automatic reflex
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain Australia's entry into WW2 as a political decision reflecting Australia's identity as a British dominion, and can explain the significance of the Menzies/Curtin contrast as marking a genuine shift in Australia's strategic identity.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain why Menzies declared Australia at war in 1939 in terms of Australia's relationship with Britain; explain the significance of Curtin's 'Australia looks to America' as a moment of strategic shift.
nodes.typical_width: Students examine Menzies' 'Australia is also at war' — explaining the constitutional and political context, not merely that the declaration was made; trace the shift in strategic orientation under Curtin as Australia faced direct threat in the Pacific; explain how the fall of Singapore in 1942 accelerated the pivot toward the USA; identify at least one way Australia's entry into WW2 differed politically from its entry into WW1.
wider: Evaluate the contrasting wartime leadership of Menzies and Curtin as a lens on how Australia's national identity and strategic priorities were contested and reshaped during the war — examining how domestic political circumstances shaped each leader's decisions

Compare Australia's strategic situation in 1942 with that of other British Dominions (Canada, New Zealand, South Africa), examining how each navigated the tension between Imperial loyalty and national interest
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 5's significance evaluation requires understanding Australian involvement as a political choice with its own logic, not an imperial reflex. Students who leave this node believing Australia 'automatically' entered because Britain did cannot evaluate the significance of Curtin's strategic pivot, cannot explain what the war changed about Australia's international relationships, and cannot engage with the K05 content on post-war significance.

response_modes.reason: Students carry from WW1 study the assumption that Australia entered because 'we're part of the empire' — this node must explicitly disrupt that framing. The scaffold is: what was Australia's constitutional and political relationship with Britain in 1939? What was Menzies choosing, and why? What changed between 1939 and 1942 to make Curtin's statement significant rather than routine?

success_criteria: Explains why Menzies declared Australia at war in terms of Australia's relationship with Britain — not merely that he did so
Explains the significance of Curtin's 'Australia looks to America' as a moment of shift in Australia's strategic identity and alliances
Identifies at least one way Australia's entry into WW2 differed politically from its entry into WW1

nodes.label: Significance of Australian involvement — evaluative integration
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate the significance of Australia's involvement in WW2 across multiple dimensions, constructing a historical argument rather than listing outcomes.
nodes.minimum_width: Students evaluate the significance of at least one aspect of Australian involvement using two distinct frames (e.g. strategic contribution; impact on Australia's relationship with Britain/USA); explain how the significance differs from that of WW1.
nodes.typical_width: Students evaluate the significance of Australian involvement across strategic, political, and national identity dimensions; draw on Nodes 1–4 to support claims about significance with causal reasoning; construct an argument that explains why the involvement mattered, not merely what it produced; examine how the war accelerated Australia's strategic reorientation from Britain to the USA.
wider: Evaluate the contrasting significance of Australian involvement as seen from different perspectives — Allied command, Australian home front, First Nations Australians serving under discriminatory conditions, POW survivors — examining how significance varies by vantage point

Compare Australia's WW2 significance with that of another Allied nation of comparable scale (Canada, New Zealand) to evaluate what was distinctive about Australia's contribution and strategic position
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Multiperspective significance analysis — examining what the war meant from different vantage points — is a genuinely rich historical thinking task. The comparison with other Dominions provides a structural scaffold for argument that extends beyond content recall.

response_modes.reason: This node integrates the inter-war causal chain (N1–N2), the diplomatic sequence (N3), and Australian political decision-making (N4) into a specific evaluative claim. Structured analytical paragraph or essay tasks that require students to draw explicitly on prior nodes work well here.

Students commonly treat significance as self-evident — 'the war was big, therefore significant.' The scaffold is explicit criteria: consequence, scale, change produced, lives affected. Applying criteria to evidence produces an argument; describing outcomes does not.

success_criteria: Evaluates the significance of Australian involvement using at least two distinct frames — not merely lists outcomes
Constructs a claim about why Australian involvement mattered, supported by evidence from the causal chain (Nodes 1–4)
Explains how WW2 changed Australia's strategic relationship with Britain and the United States
